note:
A DE moment is a point at which the direction should change. The practitioner named it on 2026-10-15, after finding that a map still had an Input mode a day after the discussion that ruled against modes: "The map output discussion is what we call a DE moment, a moment when things should head in a different direction, and it did not."

This file is the answer to that. Every direction a discussion settles is recorded here with what it requires IN CODE and a clock on it, because the failure mode is specific and this project has produced it at least three times: the direction is written into a spec page, a glossary entry or an ontology term, the code is left alone, and the record now says the matter is settled while the running application still does the old thing. A widget page is not a work item and no ratchet can see one.

It is deliberately not the blocker ledger. A blocker is a claim that something CANNOT be done yet. A direction is a decision that something SHOULD now be done differently, and the two fail in opposite ways: a blocker rots by being lifted and not noticed, a direction rots by being agreed and not built.
windowBasis: The same window the blocker ledger uses, for the same reason: this project changes in days. A direction nobody has checked in a week is a direction nobody is acting on, and saying so is the entire point of the file.

directions.inTheirWords: I think we have a misunderstanding of maps: ... A map has layers... So there is no such thing as mode, only layers
directions.requiresInCode: map_output stops having an inputMode parameter that decides which ports exist; the renderer is chosen from what is connected.

checks.found: Shipped unchanged for a day. The direction reached docs/widgets/map_output.md, the fw:layerCount vocabulary and the glossary; inputMode stayed in src/core.ts, in the Inspector and in validate-widgets.mjs, which REQUIRED four mode-keyed port declarations. The practitioner found it in the running app: "Map still has input mode", then "I thought we got rid of mode!" Built the same day: every layer port always declared, drawnMode reads the renderer from the connections, one configurable port on the node, map_output 0.10.0.

directions.statedBy: the practitioner, via the glossary withdrawal
directions.inTheirWords: It's like "carrier" which is still out there in several files (2026-10-15, naming it as the same failure as the map model)
directions.requiresInCode: The live text of the corpus stops using `carrier` and `carrier kind`. Dated records keep theirs: a withdrawn term inside one is evidence of what was thought then.
directions.workItem: docs/withdrawn-vocabulary.json#classified, and the 57 ledger uses that remain unseparated

checks.found: 146 occurrences across 45 files, exactly at the ceiling, three days after withdrawal. The ratchet forbids a NEW use and nothing makes the count fall, so the debt can sit at 146 indefinitely -- the same shape as a direction recorded and not built. What is missing is a classification: which of the 146 are dated records that may not be reworded, and which are live text that should be. The first number is a floor and the second is work. Nobody has separated them.

Classified, which is what the ceiling was missing. Of 146: 79 are dated records that may never be reworded, 57 are ledger entries not yet separated into record and live text, 6 are necessary mentions -- the ontology's own note that the term was withdrawn, and references to the fw:Carrier CLASS D11 rejected -- and 4 were live prose. The 4 were reworded to 'port type' and the ceiling fell 146 -> 142, the first time it has moved since the withdrawal. The remaining work is the 57.

directions.inTheirWords: In a DE project, we look back, we look forward, we look sideways, above and below. — and, on 2026-10-15: "105 cannot be retired as it embodies the DE approach."
directions.requiresInCode: Nothing in code. It is the stance, not a technique: back, sideways, above, below and forward, pointed at the project periodically with the previous pass's findings in hand. What it requires is USE, and that each sweep's findings land as work items rather than as a document.
directions.workItem: A sweep. Findings go to docs/todo.md, widgets/blockers.json or this register, per AGENTS.md.

checks.found: Pointed at the project twice, both on 2026-10-12 -- once over the widget set and once over vocabulary -- and not since, through three days in which the widget count, the ruleset layer, the map model and the blocker ledger all changed. The method was not withdrawn and is not in use, which is the state this file exists to make visible rather than a conclusion about whether it is worth using.

Corrected by the practitioner: "105 cannot be retired as it embodies the DE approach." This entry had offered retirement as an option and 105's own closing condition had put the whole method on the same hook as its forward prediction, so a stance read as a technique on trial. The five directions moved into AGENTS.md where the method is; 105 keeps the derivation, the three readings it first got wrong, and the dated sweeps, and its closing condition is narrowed to the prediction alone. The gap itself is unchanged and is the reason this stays open: two sweeps, both 2026-10-12, none since, through three days in which the widget set, the ruleset layer, the map model and the blocker ledger all moved.

directions.inTheirWords: BTW on 0.80 I still do not see progressive reveal. On a blank canvas, all widgets are active, does not start with Study Area. (2026-10-15)
directions.requiresInCode: The reveal rule applied to the palette a practitioner actually uses, rather than only inside the ?playback=1 view.
directions.workItem: 112, whose closing condition is now a decision: adopt the rule and under which of the three readings

checks.found: Measured under three readings on four worked examples, prototyped behind ?playback=1 with tests, and never applied to the ordinary palette -- so a blank canvas offers all 51 widgets. revealedTypes() already produces the expected behaviour at step 0, because only widgets with an empty required set are revealed on an empty canvas, which is the inputs. What is missing is the decision of WHICH reading to adopt, and that is the practitioner's; it is not missing evidence.

The practitioner, having asked twice: "I thought we implemented progressive reveal in worked examples. And used this as a progressive reveal refinement approach." Both true. The playback IS the refinement instrument -- it is what produced the three readings and the per-step measurements on four examples -- and it was reachable only by typing ?playback=1, so the person it was built for could not find it. Put in the workspace bar as "Play back the build" the same day. The ordinary palette is still untouched, which is the open part and is a decision rather than missing work.

The practitioner: "What are the three readings? This decision seems vague to make." It was, and checking why found a false premise. 112 dismissed the port rule and emptied the stage rule on the same ground -- that the first placement is already handled by STARTER_TYPES, which offers 5. Measured in the running application: a blank canvas shows 41 of 53. addableTypes starts from the starter set and then adds ALWAYS_ADDABLE (32) and the catchment types unconditionally, so the starter set is overridden two lines after it is applied. Nobody had measured the palette, only the list. So there is no three-way choice: the port rule's own numbers still dismiss it (57-82% of the palette open through a build), the receipt rule's prerequisites are unchanged, and the stage rule has content after all -- 41 to 7 on a blank canvas, which is exactly the behaviour reported missing.

directions.statedBy: the practitioner, in the 65 amendment and experiment 106
directions.inTheirWords: In a nutshell, a ruleset widget is like a mini-software program with many possibilities because of how rules may be combined to produce an output. — and, on 2026-10-15, looking at the shipped Inspector: "Regarding ruleset widgets, this is not the design we discussed, the rules are pinned not very flexible."
directions.requiresInCode: The authored form of 106 -- condition {field, comparator, value}, AND groups, OR of groups, a LIST of conclusions from the declared output vocabulary -- with a total compiler to the N3 subset 65 settled, a rule-count ceiling checkable from the form before compiling, and the Inspector authoring rules rather than choosing a pre-baked ruleset from a list of four.
directions.workItem: 106, whose closing condition is Group A green and B1 green against the three existing rulesets on their frozen fixtures

checks.found: Nothing of it is built. No comparator, no authored form, no compiler in src/rulesets.ts or src/rule-application.ts; 106 has been `asked` since 2026-10-12. What shipped is the OTHER half of 65 -- rules as declared versioned data, one widget hosting them, three widgets retired -- which is real and is not this. The practitioner meets a dropdown of four bundled rulesets whose rule text is fixed, and the only thing they can change is a declared parameter such as a 5 km threshold. "The rules are pinned" is exactly accurate. 106 says what must come first and it needs no new oracle: B1, the three existing rulesets rebuilt in the authored form and compiled, reaching identical conclusions on their frozen fixtures.

Acted on, partly, the same day. The authored form and its compiler are built in src/authored-rules.ts and B1 is GREEN: all three shipped rulesets rebuilt in the form, compiled, and reasoned under the real EYE engine reach identical conclusions. A1, A2, A3, A5, A8, A9 and A10 pass too, and the rule ceiling is checked from the form before anything is compiled. 106 moves asked -> tried. What is NOT built is the half the practitioner meets: the Inspector still offers a ruleset chosen from a list, so the rules are still pinned from where they sit. Four comparators compile and have never been executed, so by 106's own rule they must not be offered until B2 passes.

Carried further the same day, on the practitioner's proposal: "We should have a worked example just for the ruleset widget to exercise different ruleset conditions so users can also see examples of how to configure it. That is one way to execute widget rules and validate at the same time." Built as the `rulesets` workspace: three steps, one condition kind each -- a band from two comparisons, alternatives with two conclusions at once, a category match -- over twelve synthetic records chosen so every branch has one. A node can now CARRY authored rules and a generic path runs them: facts from declared field bindings, the authored form compiled, conclusions back onto the records. Two things the example found that no unit test would: the Inspector described the PINNED ruleset, so a step applying authored rules showed somebody else's title, threshold and basis; and authored rules MINT VOCABULARY -- thirty terms in one afternoon -- which now lives in urn:fieldwork:authored: so a practitioner's coinage is never mistaken for a term this application defines. The Inspector reads the rules back in plain words. What is still missing is composing them there: the rules can be read and their numbers changed, not yet written.
